hero.title: Steam Trap Failure Detection
hero.lede: Wireless, temperature-based monitoring that catches leaking, flooding, choked and isolated steam traps in real time, so the maintenance team fixes them in a day instead of waiting for the next manual audit.

kpis.label: Time to catch and correct a failed trap
Steam savings per year, per 100 traps (indicative)

why.d: With real-time detection, the time to repair or correct a failed trap drops to a single day, against much longer with manual or third-party audits. With a 10–20% steam trap failure rate, and maintenance made difficult by manpower shortage, dependence on manual or third-party skills, infrequent audits, large numbers of traps and safety concerns, the solution is an ideal fit for the maintenance team.

Inlet and outlet temperatures are monitored to detect leaking, flooding, non-operational and choked traps. A high outlet indicates leaking; a low inlet indicates flooding, a non-operational trap or choking. Saturated steam temperature is used as the baseline. On heat exchangers, control valve position is used to baseline the inlet temperature dynamically.

Traditional and imported acoustic-plus-temperature solutions bring more complexity and cost than temperature alone to reach a similar outcome, and have largely failed because of surrounding noise, installation requirements and higher cost of ownership.

No cabling. Each node carries two temperature sensors, rated up to 550 °C, mounted on the trap inlet and outlet. The node is battery powered and sends its readings to a gateway over LoRa. The gateway has a SIM card and sends data to the cloud, so the system needs zero cabling for power or communication and zero interfacing with the existing IT/OT network.

Without DCS integration the algorithm uses static baselines, since header pressure and condensate recovery do not vary much. With integration, it runs on real-time process data: header temperature and pressure, control valve position, steam flow, condensate flow and temperature, and heat exchanger process temperature.

The hardware is designed and field tested to last for many years in corrosive areas, hydrocarbon Zone 1 and all weather, with large-scale implementations in upstream and downstream refineries, pulp and fibre, and pharma. The oldest implementations have been running for more than 4 years.

failures.d: The trap has been manually isolated using its valve. Once isolated it is either choked or bypassed.
failures.impact: If choked: waterlogging that affects steam quality and may lead to water hammering. If bypassed: steam losses.

failures.d: The trap is leaking steam along with the condensate. The leak rate depends on differential pressure and orifice size.
failures.impact: Loss of expensive steam. Leak rates are very high in high-pressure header traps and in large-orifice heat exchanger traps.

failures.d: The trap cannot release the condensate. Condensate collects at the inlet and the outlet is not releasing it.
failures.impact: Affects main steam quality and process temperature, and may lead to hazardous water hammering.

failures.d: The trap cannot handle the condensate load, although it is still able to release condensate.
failures.impact: Affects header steam quality and process temperature, and may lead on to choking.

business_case.note: Assumes 100 steam traps evenly distributed across 40 bar, 24 bar, 7.5 bar and 3.5 bar pressure lines. Traps are thermodynamic (TD) type, connected to the header, with an assumed ⅛ inch orifice.
assumptions: 10–12% per year, industry standard (ranges from 5% to as much as 20%)
2.5 per pressure line, at a 10% annual failure rate
Current time to catch and correct
45 days: half of a 90-day manual audit cycle. Reduced to near zero with online detection.
plus: Better steam quality from less choking
Avoided steam bypass losses due to choking

points: Inlet and outlet RTDs are mounted on the pipe either side of the trap.
The steam trap monitoring LoRa node mounts on the nearby support pillar.
The trap discharges to the environment or to a condensate recovery line as before.
A 4G LoRa gateway is installed at height in an open location and sends data to the Faclon cloud.
Inlet and outlet temperature sensors on the trap after the heat exchanger, before the condensate recovery line.
Control valve position, header pressure (e.g. 15 bar), header temperature (e.g. 230 °C) and process temperature come from the DCS or historian.
An industrial PC sends the DCS / historian data to the Faclon cloud over 4G.
Control valve position is used to baseline the trap inlet temperature dynamically.

Online failure detection on header and heat exchanger traps, significantly reducing steam losses and improving reliability.
